_about: Field-level data for LithoHub features F1–F4. Every dataset has evidence + source. Evidence: quoted | digitized | reconstructed | illustrative | derived | pending. Well-level diagnostic data lives in assets.json.

crossSections.source: Golla et al. (2018), Figure 4, based on Rohrs et al. (2005)
crossSections.note: Schematic. Well positions are estimated from the axes of the published Figure 4 (scale ~0–8000, unit not stated in the paper), not precise pixel digitization. Thermal-cell boundaries and the clay cap are simplified.

singleWellProfile.note: The only well in the paper with a complete MD + P + T profile.

feedZoneCloud.note: Figure 7 holds ~300+ feed-zone points in 3 orthogonal projections (map view + 2 cross-sections), colored by 5 productivity-index (PI′) classes. The points are anonymous (no well identity) and matching them across the 3 projections is highly ambiguous in dense areas. This panel stays empty until digitization is done — random points labeled "illustrative" would blur the line between verified and invented data.

Cross-projection point matching with a confidence score per point (high/low)
Manual review of points with more than one equally plausible match
Explicit decision: show only the more isolated top-PI′ subset, or the whole cloud with a visual confidence indicator

trajectory3d.note: Needs wellhead coordinates (UTM), KB elevation and a directional survey (MD, inclination, azimuth) per well. Not yet found in the source papers.

fractureStats.note: 12 of 18 logged wells fall inside the commercial production boundary — only those 12 feed this analysis.

fractureRose.note: Reconstructed concentration lobe from reported strike/dip statistics (NE–SW dominant, dip > 60°) — not digitized from the original stereonet. Real per-fracture coordinates were not published.
fractureRose.method: gaussian lobe, 10° bins, symmetric about the strike axis

permeabilityAnisotropy.source: Nordquist (2017), via Kurniawan et al. (2026), SGP-TR-230, §2.2.1
permeabilityAnisotropy.note: Fracture flow is 2.5× more transmissive along strike than across it — matched grid orientation (NE) in the reservoir model.

meqReservoirBase.source: Perdana et al. (2020), WGC Reykjavik — §2, Figure 4
meqReservoirBase.note: Interpreted as imaging the stimulated/connected fracture network extent — a correlative reading of MEQ clustering, not a direct fracture count.

productivityIndex.note: Reconstructed S-curve shape matched to the documented range (280+ calibrated feed zones, PI′ 1.4×10⁻⁴ – 8×10⁻³); not digitized from the source plot.

trajectoryChecker.note: Golla et al. (2018) recommends NW or E-SE trajectories qualitatively — no exact azimuth range is published. A prior draft invented 310–320° / 110–120° cutoffs; that number was not sourced and has been removed pending a checker built directly from a measured rose diagram.

mohrCoulomb.note: Requires the full stress tensor (S_v, S_Hmax magnitude, S_hmin, pore pressure). Neither Golla (2018) nor Kurniawan (2026) publishes these magnitudes — only the S_Hmax orientation (N22°E) is known.

sibayak.name: Sibayak
sibayak.coordinateNote: Approximate field-level location for the map only — not from LithoHub source papers. Verify before publishing.

wells.source: Supriyanto et al. (2005), Table 1; injectivity index from Firanda et al. (2024)
wells.note: Each well has only two data points in the source (temperature at total depth, and maximum temperature at its depth). The chart joins them with a straight line — it is NOT a full P-T profile.
wells.columnNote: The source table gives total depth as TVD, while the maximum-temperature depth is given in m MD. Verify against the paper before mixing the two on one axis.

wells.note: No production data (exploration well). Firanda (2024) notes that the hydrostatic gradient of SBY-2 differs from the other wells — an indication of marginal recharge influence.
2024 flow rate (Firanda): 173 t/h brine + 35 t/h steam — differs from the 2005 figure, see the discrepancy panel. Deepest feed zone in the field: −405 to −425 m ASL.
Supriyanto (2005): max 170°C @ 400 m MD. Firanda (2024) describes this as the coldest well, max 124°C — the two sources have not been reconciled.

discrepancies.source: Supriyanto et al. (2005); Firanda et al. (2024)

items.resolution: Two different periods, not an error — show both with their period labels.

records.value: coldest well in the field, max 124°C

items.resolution: Not yet reconciled — do not merge into one number.

faults.source: Firanda et al. (2024), "Updating Numerical Simulation Model of Sibayak Field, Indonesia", §2
faults.note: Fault coordinates are not published numerically — only names and general orientation.
items: Singkut Caldera ring fault (main recharge path)

namedStructures.source: Firanda et al. (2024), 49th Stanford Geothermal Workshop — name-level only
namedStructures.note: Fault names were confirmed against Firanda et al. (2024) via search snippets only — the full PDF has not been read line by line. No quantitative claims (strike/dip, permeability, stress) until that verification is done.

allPanels.note: Rose diagram, effective-fracture filter and stress orientation will be added once the primary PDF is read in full and cross-checked.

faultStrikes.note: σ1 (S_Hmax) trends NNW-SSE, inferred from Riedel-shear kinematics on the mapped fault set — a structural interpretation, not an instrumented stress measurement.

compartments.source: Brehme et al. (2016), Grundwasser 21 + Suherlina et al. (2022), Table 3
compartments.note: Two compartments confirmed across independent studies: acidic / high-gas / fault-permeable vs. neutral / lower-productivity. 7 wells sampled in 2018.

referenceLineEcUsCm.note: Split line carried over from the prototype; its source is not stated — verify.

poissonRatio.source: Silitonga et al. (2005), WGC Antalya — via Qarinur et al. (2020), Table 4
poissonRatio.note: Higher ν near the surface = fractured rock; lower ν at depth = silicified, unfractured rock.

thermalForecast.note: Only the start and end values are from the source. The line between them is drawn for reading only; it is not a modeled year-by-year curve.

crossSection.source: Suherlina, Newson, Kamah & Brehme (2022), Geothermics 105 — Fig. 7, Fig. 16 & Conclusion
crossSection.note: Static schematic with hover data. No XYZ grid — not a slicing engine.

caveats.title: Fault-to-well proximity is inconsistent within the source itself
caveats.text: The Discussion section places the proven thrust fault (Fault B) near LHD 12; the Conclusion places it near LHD 8. This diagram follows the Discussion-section version.

caveats.title: The general and local framings disagree
caveats.text: At field scale, the paper states NW-SE thrust faults generally admit fluid flow to production wells, while the NE-SW fault (Fault A) is the general barrier. Only in the local LHD 8/11/12/18 compartmentalization discussion are both faults treated jointly as barriers — which is what this diagram shows.

wells.reading: Rising Cl, dropping SO₄ — boiling dry
wells.detail: Cl 347→449 mg/l (2012–2018), SO₄ falling. Shallowest feed zone; boiling due to pressure drawdown.

wells.reading: Deeper feed zone, still dries fast
wells.detail: Deeper feed zone than LHD 8 but still dries fast — depth of feed zone is not the key driver.

wells.reading: Strongest EC / Cl rise in the group
wells.detail: Shallowest feed zone of the enhanced-dryness wells; strongest chloride and EC rise in the cluster.

wells.reading: Lowered Cl, raised SO₄ — inflow signal
wells.detail: Cl 466→355 mg/l, SO₄ rising — indicates fluid inflow from the injection site. Acts differently from the drier wells on pH, EC and mass flow.
Turned into a dry-steam well by April 2018 despite the 'stable' classification from the 2013/2015 dataset.
Cl 337→193 mg/l, SO₄ rising — clearest fluid-inflow signal. Deepest feed zone of all sampled wells.

fluidModel.source: Simatupang, Matsuda & Astra (2020), Proceedings World Geothermal Congress — Fig. 15 & Conclusion
fluidModel.scopeNote: SIL is one of two producing fields in the Sarulla Complex. Namora-I-Langit (NIL), the other field, is a volcanic hydrothermal system with distributed permeability — geologically distinct from SIL's fault-controlled system. This model applies to SIL only.
fluidModel.note: Inequalities are ordinal, not magnitudes. Hover panels must not imply numeric values unless sourced separately (e.g. Simatupang 2020, Fig. 8 enthalpy–chloride cross-plot).

RB.name: Reservoir Brine (RB)
RB.detail: High H, high NCG, higher Cl, low Mg, low HCO₃. Upflow zone along the Great Sumatra Fault, T > 280°C.

IL.name: Injectate Liquid (IL)
IL.detail: Low H, higher HCO₃, low NCG. Returns from SIL 2 / SIL 3 injection pads; breakthrough detected within 2 years of production.

MR.name: Marginal Recharge (MR)
MR.detail: Low H, low Cl, high Mg, heavier δ¹⁸O. Cold lateral intrusion — not yet detected in 2-year monitoring (Mg stayed < 0.01 ppm at all wells).

relations.meaning: Enthalpy — brine is hottest, recharge coldest
Non-condensable gas — depleted in returning injectate
Bicarbonate — enriched in injectate, low in brine
Chloride — dilution signature toward the margins
Magnesium — marker for marginal recharge intrusion

slicing.note: Silangkitang and Kamojang cross-sections carry no XYZ spatial grid, so there is no dynamic slicing. If arbitrary line slicing ships later, ground it strictly in Salak's UTM grid (Golla 2018) and the 200 m × 200 m block model (Kurniawan 2026) — and first confirm that the grid carries property fields (temperature, chemistry, permeability at nodes), not just mesh geometry.

kamojang.name: Kamojang
kamojang.coordinateNote: Approximate field-level location for the map only — not from LithoHub source papers. Verify before publishing.

fieldFacts.note: Framed strictly as a steam-supply depletion indicator (reservoir matrix boiling dry) — no corrosion, HCl, HF or pH terminology appears in this source.

facts.text: Steady surface superheat rise since 2017 in the northeastern Kawah Kamojang area.
Average surface superheat drop at wells C-1, C-2 and A-2 during the 2-month C-3 pilot injection (2022).
Local pressure drop and steam loss at C-2 in the Waiwera model, from steam-column collapse under continuous central injection.

corrosionContext.note: Not applicable to Kamojang. Its published gas chemistry is CO₂/H₂S-dominated with nil-to-low chloride — not the HCl/HF profile this tier is built for. For HCl-bearing fields: steam becomes corrosive once the superheat margin drops below 24 °C; with NH₃ present that threshold rises to about 10 °C. Confirm the measurement basis (surface vs bulk superheat) before using these thresholds.
corrosionContext.thresholdsSourceNote: The 24 °C / 10 °C thresholds are carried over from the prototype without a named source in the panel — add the citation before using them.

rejectedRule.text: Fixed cutoff "ΔT > 5 °C = critical danger / corrosion risk" was dropped: unsupported by Abdurachman (2023) and directionally backwards — rising superheat widens the margin, the opposite of the acid-condensation risk direction. Kept only as an audit record.

mitigation.text: Cyclic / edgefield realignment: move injection toward the field periphery rather than continuous central infield injection, to avoid steam-column collapse — the core logic of Salak's SIRP. Applied here as an analogous strategy, not a conclusion Abdurachman (2023) reaches for Kamojang. Salak and Kamojang reservoir characteristics have not been confirmed equivalent — an untested transfer.

items: The corrosion tier assumes Kamojang gas chemistry (CO₂/H₂S-dominated, nil-to-low chloride) — needs a direct 2017–2023 chloride/HCl time series to confirm or rule out.
The 2 °C pilot-test drop has no stated control well or period — treat it as associated with, not proven caused by, the C-3 injection until confounds (rainfall, production-rate changes) are excluded.
Surface vs bulk superheat measurement basis must be confirmed consistent before comparing values near the 0 °C margin.
The mitigation transfer from Salak assumes reservoir-type equivalence not yet verified for Kamojang.
